contradictions.confidence: measured, against secondary sources of mixed quality
contradictions.claim: P-E1 SCORED: MOSTLY HOLDS, 4 OF 5 CHECKABLE CELLS WITHIN THE STAKED +/-10 POINTS, ONE OUTSIDE. The stake was 'each model's GSM8K/MATH-500/IFEval lands within +/-10 pts of its publicly reported number where one exists'. Measured: 7B IFEval 70.4 vs 70.8 (-0.4), 7B MATH-500 72.8 vs MATH 75.5 (-2.7), 4B GSM8K 81.7 vs 86.5 (-4.8), 4B IFEval 80.6 vs 89.8 (-9.2) all WITHIN; 7B GSM8K 79.9 vs 91.6 (-11.7) OUTSIDE. THE PREREG SAID WHAT TO DO ON A MISS - 'investigate placement/truncation BEFORE believing either' - and the investigation exonerates the harness. The 7B's IFEval lands 0.4 points from a published figure. A pipeline that were mis-serving, truncating or mis-scoring could not land within half a point on a 541-prompt instruction benchmark and then be 11.7 out on grade-school arithmetic. The GSM8K gap is protocol: vendor GSM8K figures are their own harness and typically few-shot CoT, ours is zero-shot on a Q4_K_M quant. That is a known-direction difference, not a defect. SOURCING IS THE WEAK PART AND IS DECLARED. Only one figure comes from a primary card (Qwen3.5-4B IFEval 89.8, huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B); the 4B GSM8K is a secondary aggregator and appears on no official card; the 7B MATH figure is MATH, not the 500-item MATH-500, and is indicative only. AND THE 4B's OWN CARD SAYS THE MODEL 'operates in thinking mode by default' without stating whether its reported scores are thinking-on. We ran --reasoning OFF throughout (protocol v2). For a thinking-by-default model that difference is larger than quantization and larger than harness, so the 4B's -9.2 'within band' result is within band for a reason the band was not designed to cover.
contradictions.magnitude: 4 of 5 within +/-10. Best agreement 7B IFEval -0.4pp; only miss 7B GSM8K -11.7pp. 0.6B and 30B not scoreable: no comparable public figures exist for those variants.
contradictions.evidence: Ours: weights/data/ev1/**/results_*.json. Public: huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B model card (PRIMARY, IFEval 89.8); Qwen2.5 official blog (GSM8K 91.6, MATH 75.5); arXiv 2605.29756 quantization study (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct IFEval avg@8 70.82 +/- 0.88); llm-stats / SaladCloud aggregators (Qwen3.5-4B GSM8K 86.5, secondary).
contradictions.scope: A SANITY CHECK, not a scientific comparison, and it should be read as one. Every cell crosses at least one protocol boundary - quantization, zero-shot vs vendor few-shot, thinking on vs off, and in one case a different evaluation set. The +/-10 band was staked to absorb 'quant + harness variance' and turned out to be absorbing something larger. NOT claimed: that any of these gaps measures quantization damage. The clean way to measure that is the byte-matched same-source pair (naive vs depth-aware), which is why that experiment exists.
contradictions.wired_into: weights/ev1_score.py prints P-E1 as NOT SCORED by the script itself, on purpose: the public figures live outside this repo and must not be hard-coded where a later reader would mistake them for measurements. The scoring is here, with its sources and its confounds, and the script points at it.

contradictions.status: resolved 2026-08-11 by prereg #99, which refuted the analysis rather than the result
contradictions.claim: I MISREAD OUR OWN BIGGEST RESULT WITHIN AN HOUR OF GETTING IT, IN THE DIRECTION THAT MADE IT SOUND MORE SOPHISTICATED. Prereg #98 confirmed P1 with MATH-500 57.0 -> 81.0 (+24.0 against a staked +2.0). The scorer also prints emitted_boxed: NAIVE 64.4% vs OURS 86.4%. From that I concluded that +22.0 of the +24.0 was ANSWER FORMATTING - that naive Q2_K had lost instruction-following rather than capability - and wrote it into the #98 scored section and commit d7910e6 as the corrected, more honest headline. It was neither. Prereg #99 re-graded both arms with lm-eval's own format-blind flexible-extract rule as a fallback on exactly the unboxed items: the gap moved +24.0 -> +23.8. FORMAT IS 1% OF IT. NAIVE recovered 2 items of 178 unboxed; OURS 1 of 68. The missing box is a lost ANSWER, not a lost format.
contradictions.resolution: THE NULL HAS POWER, which is the only reason it settles anything: 320 of 500 MATH-500 golds are purely numeric and 100 of NAIVE's 178 unboxed items have a numeric gold, so a last-number rule had up to 100 items available and took 2. The responses are also long rather than empty or truncated - median 6,787 chars, min 3,982, against 0.0% truncation on the row. Long reasoning, recoverable golds, nothing recovered. #98's P1 verdict is UNCHANGED and is better supported than under the mistaken reading. IFEval's +12.2 still stands on its own - instruction-following IS degraded - but it is a SEPARATE degradation from the MATH-500 one rather than its cause.
contradictions.mechanism: THE REUSABLE PART IS THE REASONING ERROR, NOT THE ARITHMETIC. I offered the benchmark ordering MATH-500 +24.0 > IFEval +12.2 > GSM8K +9.1 as corroboration that 'the strictest-format benchmark shows the largest gap'. It corroborates nothing: 'MATH-500 is simply the hardest of the three and degrades most' predicts the identical order, and I never stated that rival, so three points falling in a predicted order were presented as though only one hypothesis predicted them. THREE POINTS IN AN ORDER IS NOT EVIDENCE FOR A MECHANISM UNLESS THE RIVAL ORDERINGS ARE NAMED. Second-order tell, recorded because it is diagnostic: #99's own 'Why this exists' section asserts the format reading as established fact rather than as the hypothesis under test. Writing the conclusion into the motivation is how a test gets built to confirm; this one discriminated only because the extractor was chosen for provenance (a rule the project already publishes GSM8K through) and the bound was computed before running.
contradictions.evidence: prereg #99 (preregistrations/2026-08-11-format-vs-capability-decomposition.md), staked and scored the same day; weights/prereg99_score.py; the correction appended to prereg #98 (preregistrations/2026-08-09-quant-recipe-vs-naive-benchmarks.md); commits d7910e6 (the error) and 9b483ff (the retraction).
contradictions.wired_into: weights/prereg98_score.py now ALWAYS prints the format decomposition beside any boxed delta, with the sign of the reading reversed: a low emitted-box rate is evidence of capability collapse, not of a fussy scorer. The guard exists because the column was what misled me, and a column that can mislead should carry its interpretation.
contradictions.confidence: measured - 500 items per arm, one staked test, and the null was shown to have power rather than assumed to

untried.claim: THE ADDITIVE DISK-TIER FORM HAS NEVER BEEN HELD OUT ON A DEVICE, AND THAT IS THE ONLY TEST THAT WOULD LET IT SHIP AS A PREDICTION. #53 (D-27) established that `t_token = C + I` retrodicts 18 streamed phone rows across four models at 4.04% leave-one-MODEL-out, with two device constants S_c and S_i fitted on that phone's own rows. LOMO holds out a model; it never holds out a machine. So the published number answers 'can two constants explain four models on one device' and not 'can this tool tell a user with an unmeasured phone or NVMe box what they will get' - which is the only question quantprobe actually asks. The dataset that produced D-27 cannot settle it: it has one usable row on the second device, and that row already says the sequential NVMe spec is the WRONG rate (their prose calls the drive ~3 GB/s; the additive model's residual implies 0.806 GB/s effective, a 3.7x gap, and predicting at 3 GB/s overshoots by +51%). Until a device is held out, S_c and S_i are calibration inputs, not predictions, and the honest form of any shipped disk-tier advice is 'measure your machine once' rather than a number.
untried.hypothesis: Effective streamed-expert read rate S_i is a stable fraction of a device's advertised sequential bandwidth within a storage class (UFS 4.x phone, consumer NVMe), so a second device's two constants can be predicted from its class rather than fitted on its rows.
untried.predicted_effect: STAKED BEFORE ANY SECOND-DEVICE ROW IS COLLECTED. Fit S_c and S_i on device A's rows only, then predict every row of device B with N3 and NO refitting, taking S_i(B) as the same fraction of B's advertised sequential bandwidth that S_i(A) was of A's, and S_c(B) from B's memory bandwidth by Law 4 unchanged. KILL RULE: median |error| over device B's rows must come in BELOW 25% and max BELOW 60% - deliberately looser than #53's 15%/35% model-holdout gates, because a device holdout is strictly harder and staking the same numbers would be staking a failure. If either misses, the cross-device transfer of S_i is REFUTED, the disk tier stays a calibrate-then-predict tier, and quantprobe must refuse to price the streaming tier on an unmeasured machine instead of printing a number. A pass does NOT license a third device: it licenses the storage CLASS that was tested.
untried.cost: high if measured here - this box has no UFS phone and the disk tier needs a model larger than RAM. Low if the second device is obtained the way #53's first one was: a published table with per-token flash-byte instrumentation and a stated drive spec. The cheapest honest version is to ask for one (C-06's replication ask) rather than to fit one.
untried.protocol: 1) Freeze N3 and both active-byte conventions exactly as weights/exp53_two_resource_disk_tier.py has them. 2) Fit S_c, S_i on device A alone with the same deterministic grid plus coordinate descent - no RNG, no restarts. 3) Stake the transfer rule and the kill rule in a pre-registration BEFORE device B's rows are read into the scorer, and stake the predicted per-row tok/s. 4) Score device B with zero free parameters. 5) Report P-0 on device B's own models first: if the byte model does not reproduce a no-cache flash counter there, nothing downstream may be read, exactly as in #53. C-14 applies with full force - device B's rows must all carry one machine state, and a best-of table from mixed sessions makes a pass weak evidence and a failure informative.

Reducing an unmeasured machine to two rates - one of which (S_c) Law 4 already predicts from memory bandwidth - is a much smaller ask than fitting a model, and it is the last thing standing between the disk tier and an honest prediction. It also feeds C-06 directly: a second device with published per-token byte instrumentation is exactly the external replication that request has been asking for.

untried.claim: THE BINDING-RESOURCE LABEL HAS NEVER BEEN SHOWN TO PREDICT WHICH LEVER PAYS, WHICH IS THE ONLY THING IT IS PRINTED FOR. L-23 establishes that the label is not a constant, that it is internally sound, and that it reproduces BigMoeOnEdge's laptop verdict - all of which are properties of our own arithmetic plus one retrodiction we did by hand before staking it. None of that is the claim the tool makes on the page. The tool tells a user 'your box is RAM-bandwidth-bound, so a faster NVMe buys nothing', and the experiment that would refute THAT is an A/B: take a cell the classifier calls IO-bound, apply a storage upgrade, measure a real speedup; take a cell it calls bandwidth-bound, apply the SAME upgrade, measure neutral. We have exactly one such pair and it is theirs - their laptop, where I/O lanes, extra compute threads and a ~3 GB/s NVMe were all measured neutral. Two further gaps ride along and are named here rather than left to omission: prereg #88's P-3 shipped with NO kill rule at all, so all three advice probes could have come back empty and the verdict would still have read PASS; and K-1's 85% bar was never live at any bit-width we ship (worst modal share 55.9%).
untried.hypothesis: On a cell the classifier calls IO-bound, a storage-bandwidth change buys a speedup no larger than the ceiling_x the tool printed for it; on a cell it calls bandwidth-bound, the SAME change measures neutral within run-to-run noise. If both hold, the label is a diagnosis. If the second fails, it is a decoration that happens to be internally consistent.
untried.predicted_effect: STAKED BEFORE ANY ARM IS RUN, and staked as a PAIR so that a one-sided result cannot be read as a confirmation. K-7 (the A/B): on the IO-bound arm the measured speedup must be >=1.15x AND <= the printed ceiling_x; on the bandwidth-bound arm the same change must land within +/-5% of neutral. EITHER clause failing REFUTES the label as a diagnosis - the class is then demoted to printing shares and margins with no lever advice attached, and no constant (db, eta_r, rb, the 1.15/0.30 capacity thresholds) is retuned to recover it, because back-fitting the one check that faces the world destroys the only reason to run it. K-6, carried forward verbatim from prereg #88 section 8.3 and explicitly NOT applied retroactively to #54: if all three P-3 advice probes come back empty on the successor grid, the classification is decoration, the advice gates do not ship, and FINDINGS records that the shipped advice was already regime-safe. K-1 successor bars, also from section 8.3 and chosen against the distribution now known: modal share must stay <=0.60 (against 55.9% worst observed - a bar 4.1 points away, where the original 85% was 29 points away) with 4 distinct classes, since the old '3 of 4' clause was met by half the grid alone. P-4 is WITHDRAWN rather than re-staked at 0.00: 0.6% is the measured answer and re-staking a bar the result has already cleared is back-fitting wearing a prediction's clothes.
untried.cost: medium. The bandwidth-bound arm needs no new hardware - this box's all-in-VRAM and expert-split rows are bandwidth-bound and the storage change can be a cold-vs-warm page-cache contrast rather than a new drive. The IO-bound arm is the expensive half: it needs a model that genuinely streams from disk on this box, i.e. larger than RAM, which is the same 117B-class fixture the disk tier already uses. Cheaper alternative, and the one C-06 has been asking for: a second party with published per-token instrumentation runs the pair on their own box.
untried.protocol: 1) Stake the two cells, the exact storage manipulation, and the predicted per-arm outcome in a pre-registration BEFORE anything is timed - including the printed ceiling_x for the IO-bound arm, which is a deterministic output of the shipped tool and therefore costs nothing to stake and is the upper bound K-7 checks against. 2) Read both cells' classes from the shipped `quantprobe plan` output, never from a re-implementation. 3) Run both arms in ONE session under one cal_id, alternating A/B/A/B, so drift shows up as disagreement between the two A's instead of as an effect. C-14 binds with full force: the storage state must be the only thing that differs. 4) Score the pair JOINTLY - a speedup on the IO-bound arm together with a speedup on the bandwidth-bound arm is a REFUTATION, not a partial win, because it means the manipulation moved something the classifier does not model. 5) Construct the concrete input that makes the scorer report a false PASS and verify it does, before trusting the scorer; #54's own pre-run audit found five defects that way, one of which let a wrong printed share through a green gate. 6) Publish the miss at the prominence of a hit; L-23's P-4 miss is the template.
untried.why_it_is_promising: The one datapoint we have points the right way and it is not ours, which is the strongest kind: BigMoeOnEdge measured I/O lanes, thread count and a faster NVMe ALL neutral on the laptop our classifier independently calls bandwidth-bound once their own measured 80% hot-expert hit rate is substituted, and our RAM term lands within -9.2% of the compute floor they published. #54 also showed that the advice layer, not the label, is where the value has been: the upgrade advisor was drawing its counterfactual from a smaller row menu and a different model size on 31 of 340 cells - a bug that INVENTED 30 upgrade recommendations and suppressed 3 - see L-23's correction note, the 'one-directional, suppress-only' reading we first published was itself wrong - and one that stayed invisible until the per-token time was decomposed into named resources.

untried.claim: U-37 IS NOT CONFIRMED, THE PILOT'S SIGN FLIPPED ON A QUIET BOX, AND THE PREMISE TURNED OUT TO BE ABSENT. Scored 2026-08-03 on an idle machine (gate opened at CPU mean 1.7%), 5 reps per arm, each a separate llama-bench invocation. K-1 FAILED and failed BACKWARDS: R_big 0.383, i.e. --no-mmap was 2.6x SLOWER, where the staked rule needed >=1.20 FASTER. The pilot's 1.659x (contended, 2 reps) does not reproduce; contention produced it, exactly as the pilot's own caveat warned. K-2 PASSED (control 0.996 - no difference on a small model). K-3 PASSED. K-4 FAILED, and K-4 is the one that matters: minimum free RAM during the big arm was 13.49 GB, so the model never crowded memory and the residency-pressure premise was never established. NO RATIO MAY BE CLAIMED, including the 0.383. WHY THE PREMISE WAS ABSENT IS THE REAL FINDING AND IT IS AN ERROR IN MY DESIGN: I chose the 13.7 GB model as '86% of 16 GiB' from its FILE SIZE. It is a 30B-A3B MoE with ~3B active, and under mmap only the active experts fault in - free RAM sat at 13.49-13.73 GB across all five reps while the model 'ran'. File size is not resident set, and for a sparse MoE the two differ by roughly the sparsity factor. Testing residency pressure needs a DENSE model near RAM capacity; this box has none (the dense options are 8.5 GB or 37 GB). SEPARATE OBSERVATION, unscored because the run is uninformative but mechanically clear from the free-RAM trace: --no-mmap dropped free RAM to 10.75 GB, i.e. it materialised the whole file, and was 2.6x slower. On a sparse MoE --no-mmap appears actively harmful because it defeats sparse activation - paying full I/O for weights the router never touches. That is a plausible user-facing warning and it is NOT claimed here. ALSO: the big_mmap arm's 6.266x rep spread is ONE cold first rep (2.10 then 11.64-13.16, a 1.131x spread over reps 2-5), not instability - the same cherry-picking trap the gemma retraction caught, avoided here only because all five reps were printed.
untried.magnitude: R_big 1.659 vs R_small 0.955 - the residency-pressure signature, unscored
untried.evidence: weights/exp100_nommap.py + weights/data/exp100_nommap.json (the discarded wall-clock design), weights/exp100b_mmap_residency.py + weights/data/exp100b_mmap_residency.json
untried.scope: One box, one RAM size, two models, two reps per arm. Nothing here is scored and nothing may be cited as a result. Contention was present and pushes TOWARD this outcome, since memory pressure is the variable under test - which is a second reason the numbers are not claimable. The excess over L-28 is what motivated it: 1.659x exceeds L-28's 1.388x page-touch penalty, and if faulting-vs-reading were the whole story it could not.
untried.wired_into: nothing, and the hypothesis is parked rather than pursued. To revive it someone needs a DENSE model sized near RAM capacity, which this box does not have. The incidental MoE-plus---no-mmap observation is the more promising thread and would need its own stake: if --no-mmap really defeats sparse activation, that is a warning quantprobe could print whenever a user pairs --no-mmap with a MoE, and U-23's RAM-headroom gate would need an architecture condition beside its size condition.
untried.hypothesis: A model occupying most of RAM is mmap'd file-backed memory competing with the page cache for the same pages. The kernel evicts file-backed pages under pressure, so a 'warm' mmap keeps re-faulting weights it already read; malloc-backed memory (--no-mmap) is anonymous and is not reclaimed the same way. The penalty should therefore scale with model size relative to RAM and disappear well below capacity.
untried.predicted_effect: STAKED FOR THE RE-RUN, before it happens, and deliberately including the condition that would kill it. On a QUIET box, >=5 reps, decode-only throughput: K-1 median tok/s(--no-mmap) / median tok/s(mmap) >= 1.20 on a model at >=80% of RAM. K-2 the SAME ratio <= 1.10 on a model at <=30% of RAM - if the small control also shows a gap, the mechanism is mmap itself and this hypothesis is wrong. K-3 rep-to-rep spread on the large mmap arm must EXCEED the small control's spread: the hypothesis predicts instability under pressure, so a large arm that is perfectly stable refutes it. K-4 free RAM sampled per rep must confirm the large arm actually ran near capacity; if it did not, the premise is absent and no ratio may be claimed however it lands. The 2026-08-02 pilot produced 1.659 / 0.955 with spreads 1.855 vs 1.039 - matching every one of these - and is NOT counted, because it ran under contention with only 2 reps and its own KR-A (a stability requirement wrongly applied to the arm where instability is the signal) disqualified it. [SCORED 2026-08-03: K-1 FAIL (0.383, wrong direction), K-2 PASS, K-3 PASS, K-4 FAIL. Verdict UNINFORMATIVE on K-4. The design error was the model choice, not the kill rules - K-4 did its job by refusing a run whose premise was never established.]
untried.cost: ~20 minutes on an idle box; no downloads, both models already local
untried.protocol: Pre-warm both models. For each of {13.7 GB, 4.4 GB} x {mmap, no-mmap}: llama-bench -ngl 0 -n 64 -r 5, decode tok/s only (excludes load, so both arms move the same bytes on the measured path). Sample free RAM before every rep. Score medians and spreads against K-1..K-4. Stability guard on the CONTROL only.
untried.why_it_is_promising: It would convert U-23's --no-mmap RAM-headroom gate from a heuristic into a measured one, and it is the first lever found this cycle that a user can act on today with a flag they already have. It also explains an excess L-28 cannot: 1.659x is larger than L-28's 1.388x page-touch penalty, so fault cost alone cannot be the whole story.

untried.status: scored 2026-08-04 - REFUTED AS STAKED, and the sweep found something the model did not predict
untried.claim: C-06 MAY ALREADY BE EXPLAINED BY L-12, AND IF SO OUR '2x BATCHING CEILING' IS A PASCAL RESULT WE HAVE BEEN GENERALISING INTO A LAW. C-06 records that batched decode saturates at roughly 2x by about 4 concurrent slots and states that nothing this project models explains it. L-12 records that batched PREFILL converges to 65-67% of this card's FLOP ceiling, i.e. prefill here is compute-bound. Those are plausibly the same phenomenon: batching performs N times the arithmetic per weight-read, so it walks a workload from bandwidth-bound toward compute-bound, and the aggregate ceiling is min(N x BW/bytes, compute_ceiling). The crossover batch size is the ratio of the two. Computed from spec-sheet FLOPs at L-12's own 65% efficiency for a 7B at 4.5 bits: GTX 1060 crosses at batch 4.5, RTX 4090 at 32, DGX Spark at 181. C-06 measured saturation at ABOUT 4 SLOTS on the 1060. That agreement is why this is worth testing rather than filing. THE CONSEQUENCE IF IT HOLDS IS LARGER THAN THE FINDING: Law 4 is a SINGLE-STREAM model and every hardware recommendation this tool makes optimises bandwidth per byte. Above the crossover, FLOPs decide instead - so for anyone serving more than one user, or running a batch job, we may be recommending the wrong hardware entirely. It also reframes the third-party DGX Spark reports: 35-45 tok/s on a 70B Q4 is impossible at batch 1 (ceiling 6.4) but ordinary at batch 6, and a Spark's crossover is ~181.
untried.hypothesis: Batched decode is bandwidth-bound at small N and compute-bound at large N, crossing where N x (BW/bytes_per_token) meets the card's achievable FLOP throughput. C-06's 2x is not a universal batching ceiling but the specific crossover of a weak-FLOP Pascal card.
untried.predicted_effect:
STAKED BEFORE THE SWEEP. Sweep -np on a 7B all-in-VRAM on the 1060, N = 1,2,4,8,16, measuring AGGREGATE tok/s.
  K-1 aggregate must rise roughly linearly with N below the predicted crossover (4.5) and flatten above it. Specifically: aggregate(4)/aggregate(1) >= 2.5, and aggregate(16)/aggregate(8) <= 1.25.
  K-2 the measured knee must fall in N = 3-7. Outside that band the crossover arithmetic is wrong even if the shape is right, and no coefficient may be taken from it.
  K-3 REFUTATION CONDITION, stated so this can die: if aggregate never exceeds ~2x at ANY N, then C-06 is a real ceiling with a different cause, L-12 does not explain it, and this hypothesis is wrong. That is the outcome C-06 as written already predicts.
  K-4 the 7B must be all-in-VRAM so bandwidth is the only memory tier involved; a split placement would confound the crossover with the RAM tier and is not scoreable.
untried.cost: ~15 minutes on the 1060; llama-bench supports -np directly, no new harness
untried.protocol: llama-bench -m <7B Q4_K_M> -ngl 99 -n 64 -p 0 -r 3 -np {1,2,4,8,16}, aggregate tok/s per N, on an idle box. Plot aggregate vs N and locate the knee.
untried.why_it_is_promising: It would close a contradiction that has sat open as unexplained, using a law we already measured, at a cost of 15 minutes. And it opens the batched regime, which is where business workloads actually live - the 50-task suite is itself a batch job. It would also divide the disk-tier streaming penalty by the batch size, potentially a larger lever than everything in C-21 and C-23 combined.
untried.verdict: K-1 FAILED BOTH HALVES: agg(4)/agg(1) = 2.256 against a staked >=2.5, and agg(16)/agg(8) = 3.257 against a staked <=1.25. The smooth min(N x BW/bytes, FLOP-ceiling) crossover at N~4.5 is NOT what this card does, and per K-2's own language no coefficient may be taken. WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED (weights/data/u38_np_sweep.log, u38_confirm.log): aggregate decode 23.07 -> 40.07 -> 52.04 -> 53.90 across N=1,2,4,8 - which LOOKS like C-06's 2x-and-flat - then JUMPS to 175.6 at N=16 (replicated twice to 0.1%) and 219.4 at N=32. Per-stream speed falls 23.1 -> 6.7 through N=8, then RECOVERS to 11.0 at N=12-16. A smooth crossover cannot produce a per-stream recovery; a KERNEL REGIME SWITCH can (mat-vec path below some batch width, mat-mat path above it). That mechanism is a HYPOTHESIS - naming the kernels requires forcing them individually, which is the follow-up - but the discontinuity itself is measured, replicated, and was then LOCALISED by the U-39 session edge probe: N=8 gives 53.9 aggregate, N=9 gives 107.7 - the switch is exactly at the 8->9 boundary, matching llama.cpp's documented mat-vec kernel batch cap of 8 (MMVQ up to 8 rows, MMQ above). Consistent-with, not proven: kernels were not individually forced. CONSEQUENCES. (1) C-06 IS OVERTURNED - see its entry. (2) The practical headline stands regardless of mechanism: this 2016 GTX 1060 serves 32 concurrent streams of a 7B Q4_K_M at 219 aggregate tok/s, 6.9 tok/s each - 9.5x the single-stream number this project has been quoting as the card's speed. Law 4 remains a SINGLE-STREAM law; a batch axis is now evidence-backed roadmap work, not speculation. (3) The DGX Spark reframe in the original claim survives in weakened form: batched aggregates far above the single-stream ceiling are real, but our crossover arithmetic may not predict WHERE they appear on any card.

untried.claim: Batching does NOT survive expert offload the way it survives dense-in-VRAM. Staked in preregistrations/2026-08-04-u39-moe-batching.md BEFORE any batched MoE measurement on this box.
untried.verdict: MEASURED (weights/data/u39_moe_sweep.log): 30B MoE, attention+KV in VRAM, experts in RAM - aggregate decode 19.67 / 28.52 / 31.38 / 37.48 / 37.07 / 40.00 tok/s at N=1/2/4/8/16/32. P1: agg(8)/agg(1)=1.905, inside the staked [1.0,2.5]. P2: agg(32)/agg(16)=1.079, under the staked 1.5 - NO dense-style jump exists on this placement at any N up to 32. KR-A (agg(32)/agg(1)>6 would refute) came in at 2.034. KR-B valid: the dense 7B anchor hit 175.05 aggregate at N=16 in the same session, third replication of the U-38 jump (175.6, 175.8, 175.05). THE MECHANISM MODEL SURVIVES: routed-expert reads from system RAM do not amortise across streams - different users summon different experts every step - so the placement that wins single-user caps out near 2x aggregate while the dense-in-VRAM placement reaches 9.5x. PREFILL is the exception and batches fine even on the MoE (45 -> 225 tok/s, saturating by N=8): prefill is compute-bound and compute amortises; decode is expert-bandwidth-bound and does not. THE MEASURED INVERSION, now a fact not a hypothesis: at 1 user this box's best model is the 30B MoE (19.7 tok/s, far smarter than anything else that runs); at 32 users it is the dense 7B (219 aggregate vs 40 - a 5.5x throughput gap the other way). untried.claim: DRAFT-DRIVEN EXPERT PREFETCH. On the expert-offload placement the per-step cost is the SURPRISE of which experts token t+1 wants - the RAM read sits on the critical path because routing is only known after step t. But the ngram drafter already guesses tokens t+1..t+8 for free, and the router is cheap to run on drafted tokens. Run it, learn the probable expert set, and issue RAM->VRAM prefetch DURING step t. Wrong drafts waste a prefetch; correctness untouched (the real router still decides). Nearest literature: Pre-gated MoE (retrains a gate predictor), PowerInfer-class static-heat prefetch. Using the SPECULATION DRAFTS as the prefetch oracle - no retraining, no auxiliary model - appears novel. KILL RULES TO STAKE AT BUILD TIME: (a) router-on-draft expert hit-rate must beat static hot-expert caching's hit-rate on the same corpus, else this is caching with extra steps; (b) end-to-end tok/s must beat the U-39 curve at N=1 by >=15% or the PCIe traffic cost ate the win.

KR: if PCIe prefetch traffic makes decode SLOWER than no-prefetch at equal hit-rate, the mechanism is net-negative on this bus and dies.

untried.claim: EXPERT-COHERENT SAMPLING. U-39 showed MoE batching caps ~2x because lanes route to DIFFERENT experts; the residual 2x exists because lanes sometimes overlap. Make the overlap deliberate: for best-of-N on a MoE, share a greedy prefix and diverge late (or bias sampling toward agreement) so parallel samples summon overlapping expert sets per step - shared reads make the batch cheaper BECAUSE the answers agree more. Tension to measure: diversity (voting value) vs coherence (bandwidth value). Protocol sketch: batched-bench-style N=8 on the 30B offload placement, arms = independent seeds vs shared-prefix-diverge-at-75%, measure aggregate tok/s + answer diversity on suite tasks. No literature found for steering the SAMPLER to maximise expert overlap across a batch.

Every model we have ever probed is full-attention throughout. Our fragility probe is a 4-BAND DEPTH sweep, which encodes an untested assumption: that fragility is localized by DEPTH. A hybrid model with attention type spread evenly across depth is the first case that can refute it.

external.status: open
external.why: THE SHARPEST AVAILABLE TEST OF C-23, AND AN UNPROMPTED RETRODICTION HIT. airllm keeps ONE transformer layer on the GPU and streams the rest, so every token reads every weight - the purest possible instance of our streaming tier. THREE THINGS FALL OUT. (1) IT DISCRIMINATES THE C-23 MECHANISM. We measured llama.cpp streaming at 0.2505 GB/s against 0.452-0.459 for raw reads (1.82x gap) and could NOT tell mmap page-fault overhead from lower achieved throughput, because fault counts were derived from byte counts. airllm loads layers with explicit reads into a buffer, NOT mmap. If it reaches raw bandwidth, the 1.82x is mmap-specific; if it shows the same gap, the cost belongs to the streaming pattern itself. This is exactly the second-runtime datapoint C-23 lists as owed. (2) THE REPORTED SPEEDS SPAN 30x AND LAW 4 EXPLAINS THE SPREAD AS A TIER BOUNDARY, not as disagreement. Third-party reports give 0.5-2 tok/s on SSD hosts, 0.07 on a MacBook, <0.1 on HDD. For 70B at 4 bits (35 GB): if the host RAM holds it, RAM binds -> predicted 0.71 tok/s at DDR4-25 GB/s and 1.43 at DDR5-50, bracketing the reported 0.5-2; if it does not, disk binds -> predicted 0.100 (NVMe) / 0.013 (SATA) / 0.004 (HDD), bracketing the reported <0.1. BOTH REGIMES HIT with no fitting. The variable that decides which regime you are in is HOST RAM, and not one of those reports states it - which is precisely the gap quantprobe exists to close. (3) THEIR OWN NUMBER RETRODICTS ONE OF OUR LAWS. They claim 4-bit block-wise compression gives '3x inference speed up'. Law 4 predicts 4x from bytes alone (fp16 -> 4-bit); the 1.33x shortfall is dequantisation cost, which is C-02/L-16's format-class finding arriving from an independent codebase. They also report prefetch overlap buying only ~10%, consistent with I/O dominating the token rather than compute - the same shape as our disk row's 93% io term. CAVEAT ON ALL OF (2) AND (3): the 0.5-2 tok/s figures are blog and article reports, not instrumented benchmarks, and the '3x' is unsourced in the repo. Treat every number here as SOFT until measured. The retrodiction is encouraging, not scored.
external.question_to_answer: Run airllm on a model that does NOT fit host RAM, with the disk counter live, and compare achieved GB/s against the raw-read baseline on the same drive. If airllm >= ~0.45 GB/s while llama.cpp sits at 0.25, C-23's gap is mmap overhead and the fix is a runtime one. If both sit near 0.25, the cost is intrinsic to streaming and Law 4 needs a streaming-efficiency term. Secondary: does quantprobe need a 'one layer resident, stream the rest' PLACEMENT? Our menu has 'stream from disk (cold experts)' but nothing for dense layer-by-layer, which is the placement airllm popularised and which we currently cannot price at all.

external.status: scored - unit-error half stands; BYTE MODEL CORRECTED 2026-08-04 against the repo's own docs/data
external.why: TWO SEPARATE RESULTS, AND THE FIRST ONE IS A CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM AS IT REACHED US. The project was relayed to us as 'running Kimi at 10 tok/s'. Its README does not say that. It reports SECONDS PER TOKEN: quoting the raw README, 'Laptop ~32 s/token', 'Server ~19-21 s/token', and a literal run line '8 tokens in 261.5 s, 32.69 s/token average'. That is 0.031-0.053 TOKENS per second. The claim as relayed is 200-320x the reported figure, and the direction of the error is the reciprocal - s/token read as tok/s. We made the same mistake in this session's first pass and flagged the preset ladder as 'backwards' because speed appeared to FALL as RAM rose; under the correct units it rises monotonically, which is the expected direction and a signal the repo's own numbers are internally consistent. SECOND, AND THE REASON THIS IS A REGISTER ENTRY: the ladder DISCRIMINATES between Law 4 and the obvious rival model, and Law 4 wins. Architecture: 2.78T params, 93 layers, 896 routed experts, 16 active per token, experts at 4-bit, 1.56 TB checkpoint. Solving the checkpoint size for the expert/trunk split (0.5*Ex + 2*(2780-Ex) = 1560) gives experts 2667B / 1.33 TB and trunk 113B. Active experts are 16/896 of 2667B = 47.6B, i.e. 23.8 GB MUST MOVE PER TOKEN, and it moves from disk in every preset. LAW 4 PREDICTS: bytes/token is CONSTANT across presets, because which 16 of 896 experts a token needs changes every token, so the working set over a generation is the whole 1.33 TB expert store and NO preset caches a meaningful fraction of it. Therefore adding RAM should buy almost nothing. THE RIVAL MODEL - 'it is slow because it does not fit in RAM, so add RAM' - predicts speed should scale with resident set: 8.2 GB -> 128 GB is 15.6x more memory. MEASURED: 32.69 -> ~20 s/token = 1.63x. That is far nearer Law 4's 'nearly nothing' than the rival's 15.6x, and it is the whole point of the tiered model: when the binding resource is streaming bandwidth against a store you cannot cache, memory capacity is not the lever. Inverting Law 4 on each preset gives the implied effective read bandwidth: 0.73, 0.81, 0.99, 1.19 GB/s (laptop -> server). Those are physically ordinary for SCATTERED 4-bit expert reads across a 1.56 TB file on NVMe, and they sit in the same band as our own measured streaming tier (0.476 GB/s achieved on this box against 3.5 GB/s sequential; C-17/C-23). HONEST LIMIT ON THE STRENGTH OF THIS: the per-preset bandwidths are DERIVED from the measurements, not independently measured, so that half is a consistency check with one free parameter per row and is weak evidence on its own. The load-bearing result is the 1.63x vs 15.6x discrimination, which uses no free parameter. WHAT IT WOULD ACTUALLY TAKE to reach the 10 tok/s the claim asserted: 23.8 GB/token x 10 = 238 GB/s sustained against a 1.33 TB store. A DGX Spark has the bandwidth (273 GB/s) but holds 8.6% of the experts; an H100 has 3350 GB/s and holds 6.0%. You need roughly 16x H100 or ~11x Spark before the store is resident - at which point 10 tok/s is easy and the C code is irrelevant. No single-box configuration reaches it, which is exactly the kind of claim Law 4 settles without owning the hardware.

external.status: scored as arithmetic - the claim is a forced architecture reveal, not an impossibility
external.why: Pokee-Isaac 28B claims a 10M-token context on one RTX-4090-class GPU (internal RULER 93.3 at full length). Our arithmetic, no hardware needed: 24 GB minus ~16.1 GB of Q4-class 28B weights minus ~1.5 GB runtime buffers leaves ~6.4 GB of state budget, which at 10M positions is 640 BYTES per position. A standard GQA 28B-class cache (48 layers x 8 KV heads x 128 dim, f16) costs ~192 KB/pos - so the claim REQUIRES ~307x state compression (154x even at q8 KV). No KV quantization gets there; sliding-window alone cannot pass real long-range retrieval. Verdict: the claim is not impossible - it is a forced reveal that the "non-pure decoder-only architecture" must be SSM/linear-hybrid or extreme latent compression, i.e. the regime our L-24 explicitly voids for standard-attention laws. The RULER numbers are internal and unverified; stated as such. This is the E-12 method applied at announcement speed: the law prices the claim the day it ships.

external.status: reviewed 2026-08-09; TWO of its three leverage points were already ours - one refuted the same day, one refuted five days earlier. Net value is smaller and different from the entry as first written.
external.author_credit: Bidipta Sarkar, Mattie Fellows, Juan Agustin Duque et al. - FLAIR + WhiRL (Oxford), MILA, NVIDIA AI Technology Center. Senior authors Shimon Whiteson, Jakob Foerster.
external.why: THEY DERIVE ANALYTICALLY THE THING WE FOUND EMPIRICALLY, FROM THE OTHER DIRECTION. Their Appendix F computes arithmetic intensity (ops per byte moved) for batched inference and compares it to a roofline threshold = FLOPS / bandwidth. That is Law 4's physics stated from the compute side rather than the bandwidth side, and it is the frame our U-38 batching cliff and U-39 MoE cap have been missing. Their formula, reproduced exactly against their own worked example (324 for H100/bf16/m=8192/A=300), generalises to quantized weights by letting activations and weights carry different bytes-per-element.
external.magnitude: Applying their formula to OUR boxes with 4-bit weights and fp16 activations at m=4096: single-stream decode sits at 4.0 ops/byte against a roofline threshold of 71 on the RTX 3060 and 23 on the GTX 1060 - memory-bound by 18x and 6x. Batch width needed to reach the roofline: 18.3 (3060) and 5.8 (1060). Their own headline: EGGROLL reaches 91% of pure batch inference throughput vs 34% for PPO and 0.41% for OpenES, on a GH200, linear model m=8192, bf16, max batch 1024.
external.question_to_answer: Does the computed roofline crossing predict where our measured batching curves bend? U-38 put the MMVQ->MMQ kernel cliff at width 9 on the 1060, and the crossing computes to 5.8 on that same box - llama.cpp switches to the mat-mat kernel just ABOVE the point where compute starts to matter, which is either a good engineering choice or a coincidence, and we can tell which by computing the crossing for several (model, quant) shapes and checking whether the cliff tracks it.
external.evidence: Paper PDF fetched 2026-08-09; arithmetic intensity derivation in Appendix F, speed figures in Appendix E. Our numbers from re-deriving their formula with s_act=2, s_w=0.5 - the generalisation is ours, not theirs, and is arithmetic rather than measurement.
external.scope: THEIR RESULT IS ABOUT TRAINING, NOT INFERENCE, and nothing here retrodicts a tok/s figure yet. The three leverage points below are hypotheses with arithmetic behind them, not measurements. The roofline threshold also uses nominal peak FLOPS, which no real kernel reaches, so the true crossing is LOWER than computed - the numbers above are upper bounds on the batch width needed.
external.wired_into: Nothing yet. THREE LEVERAGE POINTS, in order of how cheaply they can be tested: (1) QUANTIZATION MOVES THE ROOFLINE, NOT JUST THE BYTE COUNT. At 4 bits the batch width needed to become compute-bound drops roughly 4x versus fp16, because fewer weight bytes per op raises arithmetic intensity. Law 4 currently models quantization purely as fewer bytes; this says it also changes WHICH RESOURCE BINDS. quantprobe already prints the binding constraint - it could print the batch width at which that constraint flips, which is a real advisory nobody else ships. (2) AN ANALYTIC EXPLANATION FOR U-39's MoE 2x CAP. Their 'Gaussian matrix ES' case has arithmetic intensity INDEPENDENT of batch size, because every population member reads its own weight matrix. MoE decode at batch B is the same algebra: tokens route to different experts, so the union of expert bytes read grows with B instead of being amortised. The prediction that falls out is testable and sharp - the cap should lift once B*top_k exceeds the expert count, i.e. around B=16 for a 128-expert top-8 model, because beyond that every expert is read anyway and further batching amortises normally. U-39 measured ~2.0x and stopped; this says where to look for the recovery. (3) A ROOFLINE COLUMN FOR THE BATCHING CHART. media/chart_kpi_batching_inversion already plots measured aggregate throughput against width; overlaying the computed crossing would show whether the bend is a kernel artefact or physics. LEVERAGE POINT (2) IS REFUTED, AND BY DATA THAT WAS ALREADY IN-TREE WHEN I REGISTERED IT. I predicted the MoE cap would LIFT once B*top_k saturates the expert union, around B=36 for 128 experts at top-8. weights/data/u39_moe_sweep.log already covered B up to 32 and shows a PLATEAU, not a rise: aggregate S_TG relative to B=1 goes 1.00, 1.45, 1.60, 1.91, 1.88, 2.03 for B = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The union model predicts 1.00, 1.03, 1.10, 1.24, 1.55, 2.29 - it UNDER-predicts everywhere below B=32 and then OVER-predicts at 32, and on the ratio that matters it says agg(32)/agg(16) = 1.48 where the measurement is 1.079. The shape is wrong: the real curve flattens from B=8 and the model keeps climbing. WHAT SURVIVES: the direction (MoE batching pays far less than dense) and the mechanism that expert bytes grow with batch instead of amortising. WHAT DOES NOT: that union saturation is the whole story, or that a recovery waits above B=36. THE LIKELIER EXPLANATION, now untested: these are OFFLOADED experts, so the binding resource is the host link rather than bytes-read-per-token. Once PCIe saturates, how many distinct experts the union contains stops mattering - which is why the curve flattens instead of tracking the union. That is testable against U-42's PCIe direction/balance work and is exactly the kind of thing Law 4's binding-constraint label exists to say. AND THE PROCESS POINT: I registered this hours ago as a 'sharp, testable prediction' with the falsifying data sitting in weights/data/u39_moe_sweep.log the entire time. That is C-28 committed by the entry that cites C-28. LEVERAGE POINT (3) IS NOT NEW EITHER, AND WAS ALREADY REFUTED HERE. U-38, staked and scored on 2026-08-04, is the roofline crossover applied to this exact hardware: 'batching performs N times the arithmetic per weight-read, so it walks a workload from bandwidth-bound toward compute-bound, and the aggregate ceiling is min(N x BW/bytes, compute_ceiling)'. It computed the crossover at 4.5 for the GTX 1060 on a 7B at 4.5 bits, using L-12's MEASURED 65% kernel efficiency rather than nominal peak - a better number than the 5.8 I derived from EGGROLL's appendix, because mine used spec-sheet FLOPS no real kernel reaches. U-38 was scored REFUTED AS STAKED. So the roofline framing was already tested on this box, with a more careful constant, and it did not hold. WHAT E-21 ACTUALLY CONTRIBUTES, after both corrections: (a) INDEPENDENT EXTERNAL DERIVATION of a frame we already had - confirmatory, modest, and worth citing rather than claiming; (b) the activation-versus-weight byte split in their formula, a small refinement over the single-s version, which is what let quantization be priced separately; (c) their own measured throughput figures (91% / 34% / 0.41% of batch-inference throughput on a GH200) as an external datapoint; and (d) THE STRATEGIC RISK, which is the only genuinely new thing here and remains untouched by either correction: ES needs no differentiability, so it can train a model directly in the datatype it is served in - EGG, all weights int8, nonlinearity from int8 clipping alone, beating an fp32 backprop Transformer at 3.40 vs 3.58 bits/byte. If natively-low-bit training scales, post-hoc quantization recipes matter less. THE PROCESS FAILURE, stated once: I read an external paper and mapped it onto our work WITHOUT FIRST READING WHAT OUR WORK ALREADY CONTAINED. Two of the three 'leverage points' were re-derivations of in-tree findings, one already refuted by data in weights/data and one already refuted by a scored pre-registration. The register is 160 entries and searchable, and checking it is cheaper than the arithmetic I did instead. An external paper is most dangerous when it is genuinely good, because agreement with a frame you already hold reads as confirmation rather than as the duplicate it is.
external.priority: high - (1) and (2) are arithmetic we can do today with no GPU, and (2) turns a measured dead end into a falsifiable prediction. THE STRATEGIC RISK IS WORTH NAMING TOO, because it runs against this project's premise: they train EGG, a nonlinear RNN language model with ALL WEIGHTS IN int8 and no activation function beyond int8 clipping, and it beats an fp32 backprop Transformer on test cross-entropy (3.40 vs 3.58 bits/byte). ES does not need differentiability, so it can optimise a model directly in the datatype it will be served in. If natively-low-bit training scales, post-hoc quantization recipes - our product - matter less, because there is nothing to recover. That is a small-scale result today and a direction worth watching rather than a refutation, but pretending it is not aimed at us would be exactly the kind of comfortable reading this register exists to prevent.

external.repo: arXiv:2512.08296 - Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems (Kim et al., Google Research + academic)

external.status: reviewed 2026-08-15; masked 'eviction' moves no bytes - a clean Law-4 corollary
external.repo: arXiv:2608.01247 (RestoreKV, Baek et al.) + NVIDIA/kvpress artifact; measured by @superalesha
external.why: A STRANGER PRACTICING C-28. @superalesha tested kvpress's '16x KV compression' on 2x3090: resident VRAM 17.8 GB after 'compressing' vs 17.5 GB full - zero bytes freed, and decode 1.9x SLOWER. Source dive: kvzip picks evictions by global top-k across heads, giving a RAGGED cache that will not fit a rectangular tensor, so kvpress keeps everything and MASKS the dead keys with fakes that get zero attention - quality behaves as if evicted, memory never moves. His snapkv control is airtight and I re-checked the arithmetic: 16,280->1,017 tokens freed 2.1 GB = 147.7 KB/token against Qwen3's computed 144 (2.6%, allocator granularity) - his harness provably sees real eviction, so kvpress freeing nothing is kvpress's property, not his rig's. THE LAW-4 COROLLARY: masking keeps the bytes resident AND still streams them through attention every step, so NEITHER capacity NOR bandwidth moves - compression that does not move bytes moves only quality. Distinguishes our KV advice (llama.cpp -ctk/-ctv q8_0 genuinely halves the allocation, U-01) from masked-simulation tools; worth one doc sentence so a reader never maps our advice onto a kvpress-class artifact. The RestoreKV quality claim replicates (41->74 vs the paper's 38->73 at 20x).
external.magnitude: '16x compression' frees 0 bytes and costs 1.9x; the byte-movement test is the whole discriminator
